Thank you for submitting your article "High-resolution and high-accuracy topographic and transcriptional maps of the nucleosome barrier" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Jessica Tyler as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

Chen et al. address the question of how Pol II transcribes through the nucleosome, what does its energy landscape look like, and how is it modified by epigenetic markers. They combine two single-molecule assays, DNA unzipping and transcription translocation, to probe the sequence-dependence of nucleosome unwrapping and transcription elongating. An impressive combination of technical innovations allowed them to achieve single base pair accuracy in both assays. Additional unzipping barriers due to the nucleosome were identified, predominantly at the proximal side. Histone variants H2A.Z and uH2B yielded different, larger barriers. A significant increase in pausing during transcription was observed when the substrate contained a nucleosome. Importantly, the location and amplitude of the pauses could be related to the unzipping energy landscape, and using a sophisticated model, a dwell-time distribution as well as an energy landscape for transcription along the nucleosome could be reconstructed. Though both H2A.Z and uH2B nucleosomes slowed down transcription relative to wild type nucleosomes, they introduce different modifications to the energy landscape: H2A.Z introduces a broader distribution of barriers to transcription whereas uH2B increases the height of some of the barriers.

This manuscript describes a major advance in the field. Technically, the accuracy improvements of both assays are significant and allow for a much more detailed interpretation of the data than was reported before. The reported hopping behavior of nucleosomal unwrapping for example has not been observed with such precision.

The molecular mechanisms that are extracted, including detailed energy landscapes, are new and provide the field with a detailed reference for other processes that involve nucleosome transactions.

The impact on our understanding of the biology is significant: the detailed insight reported here provides mechanistic, rather than correlational or kinetic understanding of epigenetic modifications.

Major point:

Regarding the analysis method used to construct the topographic maps (e.g., Figure 1): They point out that the dwell time for each force-vs.-extension contour reflects the strength of the local histone-DNA interaction. As they also point out, what really matters is the force where the transition occurs. The higher the transition force, yes, the longer the dwell time. But also the dwell time depends on where the force began, which depends on both the previous transition force and the amount of DNA released (gives the size of the resultant force drop). All the transitions are in a similar force range and the amount of released DNA vary by factors of 2-4. So it seems that the reported dwell times for a given rupture are just as dependent on how far the previous rupture dropped in force as they are on the magnitude of their own rupture force. This would create a strong convolution and severely scramble the conclusions drawn from the map. For example, in Figure 1C of hWT unzipping, we see two distinct ruptures at very high force near 30 pN. The first rupture has a very long dwell time because the preceding rupture occurred at only 22 pN, while the second has a very short dwell despite needing also 30 pN to rupture because the preceding rupture also occurred at 30 pN. So while these two transitions which required similarly high force to rupture get scored by this method very differently, with the second appearing as a very weak interaction. It seems they are aware of the possibility of such an underestimation of the interaction. But the same effects also overestimate the first rupture. Why can they not measure the distribution of rupture forces (similar to protein folding force spectroscopy methods) directly? Otherwise, they should validate their analysis method on e.g., a long well modeled hairpin or provide some better justification that the conclusions from this method are not seriously flawed.

Reviewer #2:

This paper presents some very lovely high-resolution measurements of DNA unwrapping from various nucleosome configurations as well as Pol II transcribing through the same nucleosomes. The experimental method of pulling DNA off of the nucleosome by unwinding it from one end is very cool, though I have some concerns about the analysis methods to produce the so-called topographic map. The transcriptional map experiments seem very well done and seem like a very significant advancement. It seems like these are the most important measurements in the manuscript and they are mostly supported by the topography experiments (see my concerns about those below). It is not clear that the topography experiments themselves are necessary to interpret the transcription experiments. It is very exciting to see the distinct differences in the effects that H2A.Z vs. uH2B have on Pol II. The mechanical modeling seems sound. Overall, the paper is very strong and exciting and should be suitable to publication in eLife with the following analysis and interpretation concerns adequately addressed.

I have a serious concern regarding the analysis method used to construct the topographic maps (e.g., Figure 1). They point out that the dwell time for each force-vs.-extension contour reflects the strength of the local histone-DNA interaction. They also point out one complication: What really matters is the force where the transition occurs. The higher the transition force, yes, the longer the dwell time. But also the dwell time depends on where the force began, which depends on both the previous transition force and the amount of DNA released (gives the size of the resultant force drop). All the transitions are in a similar force range and the amount of released DNA vary by factors of 2-4. So it seems that the reported dwell times for a given rupture are just as dependent on how far the previous rupture dropped in force as they are on the magnitude of their own rupture force. I am concerned that this would create a strong convolution and severely scramble the conclusions drawn from the map. E.g., for Figure 1C, hWT unzipping, we see two distinct ruptures at very high force near 30 pN. The first rupture has a very long dwell time because the preceding rupture occurred at only 22 pN, while the second has a very short dwell despite needing also 30 pN to rupture because the preceding rupture also occurred at 30 pN. So while these two transitions which required similarly high force to rupture get scored by this method very differently, with the second appearing as a very weak interaction. It seems they are aware of the possibility of such an underestimation of the interaction. But the same effects also overestimate the first rupture. Why can they not measure the distribution of rupture forces (similar to protein folding force spectroscopy methods) directly? Otherwise, they should validate their analysis method on e.g., a long well modeled hairpin or provide some better justification that the conclusions from this method are not seriously flawed.

I think there is some unnecessary confusion in the descriptions of the initial force-extension method. From the initial presentation, it seems pulling on the NPS only is done very near equilibrium since it is shown that there is no hysteresis comparing pulling and relaxing. Later though, hopping is discussed and whether it is seen in the pulling curves and claim they pulled fast enough to not get hopping, i.e., out of equilibrium. But they say they do sometimes see hopping, for nucleosome pulling curves. This seems confusing and possibly contradictory. But either way, pulling curves should be shown plotted with sufficient bandwidth to say much about whether hopping does or doesn't occur. Hopping of bare hairpin DNA (no nucleosome) can be very fast, and the lack of hysteresis strongly suggests it is occurring faster than plotted. It would be helpful to the reader if they more clearly explained the pulling conditions and how the force ramp rate (pN/s) rather than trap displacement speed (nm/s) relates to the scale of unzipping and re-zipping times.

claims.claim: The real-time characterization of the dynamics of Pol II molecules traversing through nucleosomes at the highest resolution and accuracy reported so far constitutes important steps towards uncovering the physical mechanisms underpinning the regulation of eukaryotic gene expression.
claims.source: More broadly, the real-time characterization of the dynamics of Pol II molecules traversing through nucleosomes at the highest resolution and accuracy reported so far, and the resulting nucleosome transcriptional map, constitute important steps towards uncovering the physical mechanisms underpinning the regulation of eukaryotic gene expression.
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim about the significance of the work.

results.result: The authors developed a high-resolution single-molecule DNA unzipping assay using optical tweezers to map nucleosome topography. The assay uses two consecutive '601' nucleosome positioning sequences (NPS) that produce highly reproducible force-extension signatures, enabling precise alignment of traces from different experiments. Complete histone removal occurred in ~75% of cases after full unzipping.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C29 describe the experimental design and basic observations from the unzipping assay. The use of consecutive NPS sequences for alignment (C27) is well-supported by the reproducibility shown in figures. The quantitative observation of 75% complete histone removal (C28) is directly measured. The technical approach addresses previous limitations in the field.

results.result: Topographic mapping reveals that the unzipping fork encounters substantial resistance at specific positions (17, 26, 31, 41, 52, 61, 69 bp) corresponding to histone-DNA interactions, with resistance diminishing significantly after the dyad. The observed 5-10 bp periodicity reflects histone-DNA contacts along the DNA minor groove.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C34 present the core topographic findings from both constant velocity and constant force unzipping experiments (Figures 1E, 2B). The specific positions of resistance peaks are directly measured, and the periodicity observation (C33) is consistent with previous work and structural data. The interpretation regarding the dyad asymmetry (C32) is supported by the data.

results.result: Tetrasome unzipping reveals a substantially diminished barrier compared to octamers, with dwelling events restricted to the dyad region. This demonstrates that H2A/H2B dimers not only interact locally with DNA but also affect H3/H4 tetramer-DNA interactions near the dyad, highlighting non-local histone-DNA interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 are well-supported by the tetrasome unzipping data (Figure 1E). The comparison between octamer and tetrasome clearly shows the contribution of H2A/H2B dimers. The interpretation of non-local interactions (C36) is reasonable given the data, and the biological relevance (C37) is supported by appropriate citations.

results.result: H2A.Z and uH2B nucleosomes show distinct topographic alterations: uH2B stabilizes the dimer region (16 and 25 bp peaks) with minor effects on the tetramer region, while H2A.Z shows enhanced peaks at 41 and 52 bp with lower heights at 25 and 31 bp. H2A.Z nucleosomes display more broadly distributed dwell-time peaks and have on average one more transition per trace than WT.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41 describe the differential effects of histone modifications on nucleosome topography, supported by data in Figures 1E and 2B. The quantitative observation of additional transitions in H2A.Z (C41) is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F. The interpretations about barrier height vs. width are consistent with the experimental observations.

results.result: H2A.Z nucleosomes show no enhanced lateral mobility in partial unzipping-rezipping experiments, contradicting previous reports. Instead, H2A.Z redistributes barrier strength across the nucleosome, effectively broadening it. The H2A.Z octamer is more stable than WT, with significantly less hexasome formation during assembly. The M3 and M7 regions within H2A.Z are important for conferring increased octamer stability.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C48 address the mechanism of H2A.Z effects. The lack of lateral mobility (C42) is directly shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-H and contradicts Rudnizky et al. 2016. The assembly cooperativity data (C45) is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, and the swap mutant experiments (C46) identify specific regions responsible. The structural interpretations (C47-C48) are supported by appropriate citations.

results.result: Nucleosome-specific hopping dynamics are observed in the proximal dimer region during unzipping. These reversible transitions contrast with irreversible transitions deeper in the nucleosome. WT nucleosomes display an additional peak in the distribution of unzipped base pairs at approximately 28 bp, corresponding to H2A-H2B dimer contacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 describe hopping dynamics observed in equilibrium experiments. The nucleosome-specificity (C49) is demonstrated by comparison with bare DNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B). The additional peak at 28 bp (C51) is clearly shown in Figure 3C and corresponds to known dimer-DNA contacts. The interpretation of reversible vs. irreversible transitions (C50) is reasonable.

results.result: A 'molecular ruler' consisting of eight tandem repeats of 64 bp DNA with a single sequence-encoded pause site enables accurate positioning of Pol II along the template. The repeating pausing patterns generate a periodicity of 21.1 ± 0.3 nm, corresponding to 64 bp under experimental conditions. This tethering geometry is superior to prior designs by isolating Pol II from bead surfaces.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 describe the key methodological innovation for transcription experiments. The molecular ruler design is validated by bulk and single-molecule data (Figure 4 and supplements). The measured periodicity (C53) is quantitative and precise. The claim about superiority (C54) is supported by citation regarding photo-damage, though direct comparison data is not shown.

results.result: Pol II transcription through bare NPS DNA shows a median crossing time of 11 s, pause-free velocity of 28.9 ± 3.0 nt/s, and minimal backtracking (0.17 events per trace). In contrast, Xenopus WT nucleosomes cause dramatic slowdown with median crossing time of 129 s, reduced pause-free velocity (11.4 ± 4.1 nt/s), and 59% crossing probability. These measurements represent nearly 20-fold improvement in resolution and accuracy over previous studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60 present baseline transcription measurements and the improvement over previous work. All quantitative values are directly measured and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The comparison to previous work (C60) is supported by appropriate citations. The dramatic difference between bare DNA and nucleosome conditions validates the experimental system.

results.result: The transcriptional barrier begins immediately when Pol II touches the NPS (3 bp), is strongest at 28 bp and 10-20 bp before the dyad, and becomes negligible after the dyad. A critical region between 28-64 bp shows long-lived pauses with ~10 bp periodicity (28, 38, 48, 57, 64 bp) and frequent backtracking. This region coincides with maximum resistance in unzipping assays and may serve as an important regulatory checkpoint, as molecules that cross it typically reach the stall site.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C68 describe the detailed transcriptional map from Figure 6A and related data. The specific pause positions and their periodicity (C64-C65) are directly observed across multiple molecules. The correlation with unzipping data (C66) strengthens the interpretation. The speculation about regulatory function (C68) is reasonable given the arrest data (C67), though it remains a hypothesis requiring further testing.

results.result: The transcriptional map asymmetry is observed in both transcription and unzipping experiments, suggesting it reflects intrinsic nucleosome properties rather than polymerase bulk. Human nucleosomes confer significantly higher barriers than Xenopus nucleosomes in the proximal dimer region (28 bp peak). Pol II hopping at 28 bp coincides with unzipping fork hopping and likely reflects sampling of alternative nucleosomal states, while hopping at 63 bp may involve Pol II-histone interactions or nucleosome re-wrapping.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C72 compare different experimental observations and propose mechanistic interpretations. The comparison between transcription and unzipping asymmetry (C69) is data-driven. The species difference (C70) is clearly shown in Figure 6A. The interpretations of hopping dynamics (C71-C72) are reasonable hypotheses based on the data, with C72 explicitly presented as speculation.

results.result: After exiting the nucleosome, Pol II pause-free velocity resumes to 70% of its pre-crossing value. Nucleosome reassembly after Pol II traversal is inefficient (<5%) under the assay conditions, similar to bulk transcription assays without factors like FACT.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 describe post-crossing observations. The velocity measurement (C73) is quantitative and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1H. The low reassembly efficiency (C74) is directly observed and consistent with previous bulk studies (C75), supported by appropriate citation. These observations validate the experimental system.

results.result: H2A.Z nucleosomes show similar crossing probability to WT (58% vs 59%) but cause global redistribution of Pol II pause sites along the entire NPS. The scattered distribution (3, 28, 36, 59, 66, 87, 101, 115, 125, 138 bp) differs significantly from WT (3, 28, 57, 64 bp) where most pauses occur before the dyad. The consistent first pause at ~3 bp in all H2A.Z trajectories rules out nucleosome mispositioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 describe H2A.Z effects on transcription dynamics. The crossing probabilities (C76) are quantitative measurements from Figure 6—figure supplement 1F. The redistribution of pause sites (C77-C78) is clearly shown in Figure 6A. The control observation about the 3 bp pause (C79) effectively rules out an alternative explanation, strengthening the interpretation.

results.result: uH2B nucleosomes show slightly higher crossing probability (76%) than hWT but with longer crossing times. The median dwell-time at pause sites near the dyad is more than double that of WT, suggesting enhanced barrier height. Overall pause-free velocities are lower for both H2A.Z (11.4 ± 7.1 nt/s) and uH2B (12.9 ± 3.4 nt/s) compared to hWT (18.2 ± 7.1 nt/s), resulting in longer median crossing times (H2A.Z: 262 s, uH2B: 304 s vs hWT: 230 s). Backtrack durations are longer for H2A.Z, and arrest positions are more scattered for both modifications.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C86 present comprehensive quantitative comparisons of modified nucleosomes. All values are directly measured and shown in Figure 6 and supplements. The interpretation that uH2B enhances barrier height (C81) is supported by the dwell-time data. The backtracking analysis (C85) from Supplementary file 2 adds mechanistic detail. The scattered arrest positions (C86) are shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

results.result: H2A.Z mainly enhances barrier width while uH2B mainly enhances barrier height, both resulting in stronger barriers than WT nucleosomes for Pol II. uH2B nucleosomes pose higher barrier magnitude especially near the dyad, consistent with previously reported higher stability. For WT and H2A.Z, the transcriptional map replicates the topography map, but not for uH2B, suggesting uH2B-Pol II specific interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C91 synthesize the main findings about histone modifications. The width vs. height distinction (C87) is well-supported by the comprehensive data from both unzipping and transcription experiments. The consistency with previous stability reports (C88) is appropriately cited. The observation about map correspondence (C89) is insightful and suggests additional complexity for uH2B that warrants future investigation.

results.result: A mechanical model assumes Pol II cannot actively separate DNA from the octamer but behaves as a ratchet rectifying DNA unwrapping fluctuations. The model predicts that interaction energies necessary to generate observed dwell-time profiles are similar in magnitude for all three nucleosomal types. However, wider peaks of strong binding cause increased pause durations in uH2B, while many narrower peaks account for increased pausing sites in H2A.Z.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 describe the mechanical model and its predictions. The model assumptions (C92-C93) are clearly stated and build on previous work. The fitting results (C94-C96) shown in Figure 7D-E demonstrate that the model can recapitulate experimental observations. The model provides a quantitative framework for understanding how different energy landscapes produce different transcriptional behaviors, though it remains a simplified representation.

results.result: The proximal dimer region (~28 bp, SHL-5) is identified as a major physical barrier and potential regulatory checkpoint for Pol II. Pausing at this location shows extensive hopping dynamics, likely reflecting DNA unwrapping/rewrapping and nucleosomal rearrangements. The location coincides with partially unwrapped intermediates detected by other methods. The high-resolution data indicates the proximal dimer region, not the dyad, represents the highest barrier, providing a time window for regulatory factor binding such as FACT.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C105 present key mechanistic conclusions. The identification of the proximal dimer as the major barrier (C97, C102) is well-supported by both unzipping and transcription data. The connection to structural intermediates (C100-C101) is supported by appropriate citations. The speculation about regulatory function (C98, C103) is reasonable given the data but remains hypothetical. The FACT example (C104) is appropriately cited but not experimentally tested here.

results.result: The topographic map of WT and H2A.Z barriers before the dyad closely parallels the transcriptional map, indicating that barrier crossing is dictated by energetic requirements of disrupting DNA-histone interactions. H2A.Z redistributes barrier strength across and beyond the dyad, effectively increasing width rather than height. This redistribution provides more opportunities for Pol II to pause and interact with regulatory factors. The strong H2A.Z barrier may explain its role in poising quiescent genes in yeast and prevalence in +1 nucleosomes, while facilitation of transcription in multicellular organisms likely involves trans-acting factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C113 synthesize findings about H2A.Z mechanism and biological implications. The parallel between topographic and transcriptional maps (C106) is well-demonstrated. The redistribution interpretation (C108-C110) is supported by comprehensive data. The biological interpretations (C112-C113) appropriately connect in vitro findings to in vivo observations through citations, though they acknowledge species-specific differences and the likely involvement of additional factors.

results.result: uH2B strengthens histone-DNA interactions at the dimer region and increases overall barrier strength to Pol II, with effects propagating to other nucleosome regions including near the dyad. In vivo, H2B ubiquitination is highly dynamic, and higher levels of H2A.Z and uH2B are observed in transcriptionally silent promoters in yeast. The results demonstrate that H2A.Z and uH2B provide orthogonal means to enhance the transcription barrier, contributing to transcriptional ground state maintenance and gene silencing, while also exerting direct effects on Pol II transcription dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C120 synthesize uH2B findings and connect to biological function. The in vitro observations (C114-C115) are well-supported by the experimental data. The in vivo context (C116-C118) is appropriately cited. The conclusion about orthogonal barrier enhancement (C119) effectively integrates the current findings with previous genomic observations. The statement about direct effects (C120) is important as it demonstrates that modifications can act independently of trans-acting factors.

results.result: The mechanical model is general and should prove useful for predicting Pol II behavior through alternative barriers. The authors acknowledge that in vivo transcription dynamics are affected by numerous additional factors including higher-order chromatin folding, DNA topology, and transcription regulators. The real-time characterization at unprecedented resolution and accuracy constitutes important steps toward uncovering physical mechanisms of eukaryotic gene expression regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C124 provide appropriate context and perspective on the work. The claim about model utility (C121) is reasonable given its success in fitting the data. The acknowledgment of additional in vivo factors (C122) appropriately recognizes the limitations of the in vitro system. The summary statement (C124) accurately reflects the significance of the technical and conceptual advances while appropriately positioning them as steps toward fuller understanding.
